name: Menthyl lactate
lead: Menthyl lactate is an ester of menthol and lactic acid used as a cooling agent, giving a milder and longer-lasting cooling sensation than menthol in product formulations described in patents.[1][2] It appears in cosmetics, fragrances, oral-care and tobacco products.[3][4]

It is relevant to skincare mainly as a sensorial ingredient (a cooling or soothing feel) rather than as an agent with a documented effect on appearance. Published literature on it is sparse: the sources reviewed consist of a fragrance safety assessment, a study of coolants in tobacco, patents and an unrelated conservation-science preprint.
infobox: Cosmetics, fragrance, oral care, tobacco flavoring

paras: Patent filings describe menthyl lactate and related lactoyl esters as physiological coolants and as menthol replacements in consumer products.[1][2] The International Fragrance Association's research institute (RIFM) has published a safety assessment for l-menthyl lactate as a fragrance ingredient.[3] A 2025 study of notifications to EU member states found synthetic coolants in cigarettes and heated tobacco products, in the context of the EU ban on characterising flavours such as menthol.[4] Outside consumer products, a 2025 preprint describes using it as a volatile binder to consolidate a damaged wooden crucifix for transport.[5]

No studies found for menthyl lactate as an appearance or skincare ingredient. A registered phase 4 trial examined oral sprays and salivary pH, but the sources reviewed do not describe results for menthyl lactate specifically.[6]
Safety evaluation in the sources reviewed is limited to the RIFM fragrance-ingredient assessment.[3] The sources do not report adverse-event data from skincare use.

card.summary: Menthol-derived cooling ingredient used for feel in cosmetics; no evidence it changes appearance.
card.note: Little published research; sensorial rather than cosmetic-effect ingredient.

quick.overview:
Menthyl lactate is a menthol-lactic acid ester used to give products a cooling feel. It appears in cosmetics, fragrances, oral care and some tobacco products.

No published study in the sources reviewed tests it for any appearance outcome.
quick.mechanism: Patents describe it as a physiological coolant that produces a cooling sensation, with properties compared to menthol.
quick.risks: The main safety document in the sources is a RIFM fragrance-ingredient assessment. Little other safety literature on skincare use was found.
